source: In the S bus, in the rush hour. A chap of about 26, felt hat with a cord instead of a ribbon, neck too long, as if someone’s been having a tug-of-war with it. People getting off. The chap in question gets annoyed with one of the men standing next to him. He accuses him of jostling him every time anyone goes past. A snivelling tone which is meant to be aggressive. When he sees a vacant seat he throws himself on to it. Two hours later, I meet him in the Cour de Rome, in front of the gare Saint-Lazare. He’s with a friend who’s saying: "You ought to get an extra button put on your overcoat." He shows him where (at the lapels) and why.

gens.text: In the hospital's emergency wing, a cluster of chairs lines the waiting area. Monitors beep rhythmically, IV drips steady, and a curtain conceals a patient in distress, moaning softly. Beside them, a companion paces, their frustration palpable, complaining bitterly about the interminable wait. Pages crackle over the intercom, summoning staff to various stations, while forms and wristbands denote the urgency of each case. The scene is a whirl of controlled chaos, each moment critical. Meanwhile, the nurse at the desk updates the patient's chart, her eyes scanning the room, coordinating the flow. Inside the treatment bay, the doctor reassures the patient, their calm demeanor a contrast to the surrounding commotion. Suddenly, a monitor alarms, drawing everyone's attention.
